utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, would you please stand and make the solemn declaration in the document which the Court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, madam. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would ask that the witness be shown her pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P82 and it will be under seal. Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 81, I'm going to ask you to look at that piece of paper in front of you and ask you if that is your name on the top line of that sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your date of birth on the second line of that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's all right; it will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the purposes of concealing your identity, we're going to be referring to you as Witness Number 81. If you need to refer to any other witnesses, I'd ask you to refer to the sheet below and use their number. I'd ask you to begin your testimony here this morning, would you briefly describe for the Chamber what your educational background is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I completed a secondary technical school for typists, secretary typist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without telling us where you worked, is it fair to say that you were a professional working woman in the years around 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a business in that town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there -- was there a point in time in the spring of 1992 or early summer of 1992 that you moved from one area of Visegrad to another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what area you moved to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: First I moved to Gorazde, then I went back, and then again I moved to a neighbourhood, a suburban area near Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the name of that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how far is Kosovo Polje from the centre of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Less than two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how far is Kosovo Polje from Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Well, two kilometres and between three and four hundred metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in describing Kosovo Polje as one of the first areas outside of Visegrad that is rural, that is made up primarily of farming fields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, do you know a person by the name of Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to describe for the Court how it is you know a person by this name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic lives halfway between Visegrad and Kosovo Polje, where I would pass by on a daily basis when going to work and once, when I got married, when going to visit my parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you estimate for us what year it was when you first came to know this person as Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Since Mr. Vasiljevic's parents had a house there, I had known Mitar for at least 15 years prior to 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on January 18th of this year, did there come a time when you were asked to view a number of photographs by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recognise anybody in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes. I instantly recognised Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For what purpose, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to place the photo array on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now back in public session. Yes. Is there any objection to the tender of that document, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be Exhibit P20-81 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you first saw that set of pictures, was there any writing of any kind on those pictures? Witness 81, at the time you first saw those pictures, did you see any writing on the pictures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look around the courtroom today and ask you, do you recognise anybody in this courtroom here this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Mr. Mitar. I'm sorry. When I saw him I just got lost for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe who you're identifying at this point in time, using their first and last name, and describe where they're sitting and what they're wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: He's wearing a brown suit, headphones, and I think he's sitting behind his counsel, as far as I can understand, next to one of your police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the full name of the person you are now indicating to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect she has identified the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the latter part of April in 1992 and ask you, did you have occasion or interaction with Mr. Vasiljevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: In the month of April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: No, but -- yes, in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe what occurred in May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, 1992, Visegrad was abandoned by the former JNA. That is, the former JNA left the town of Visegrad and withdrew to the outskirts of the town. On the following day, I went with my family to Kosovo Polje with the intention to work on our land, and I was carrying a wicker basket with some seeds. And at the entrance, at the gate of Mr. Vasiljevic's house, there stood Mitar with his wife and three unknown uniformed individuals, wearing former JNA uniforms, that is. At that moment, Mitar Vasiljevic approached us with his wife and they wanted me to show them my identity card. I handed over my identity card to Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic and he asked me when I intended to come back from Kosovo Polje. And I said, "Around 1800." He kept my identity card and he told me, and I quote: "Don't let me look for you." I left for Kosovo Polje with the intention of avoiding what I had already experienced in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this occur -- the house that you're referring to, was that on the road between Visegrad and Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It happened in front of the entrance, in front of the gate to Mitar Vasiljevic's yard, to the yard of his house. There was a creek on the left side which passes along the house belonging to the Sisic family, which is the adjacent house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what road this house is on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: On the road to Visegrad, towards Kosovo Polje, on the right side, and opposite -- across the street from Mr. Vasiljevic's house, there are no houses at all along the distance of some 200 or 300 metres. There are no houses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time of the day is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was Mr. Vasiljevic dressed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: He was wearing his waiter's uniform, a black waiter's uniform, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have any weapons that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Mitar and the three other individuals had rifles. They were armed. Whereas his wife, Milojka, she didn't have any. She was just wearing her ordinary civilian clothes, ladies' clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other three men that you're describing being present at this time, did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: No, I didn't recognise any of them. I don't think that they were from Visegrad. I wasn't able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to a time just before the Muslim holiday of Kurban Bajram. Did you have occasion to see Mr. Vasiljevic around that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I remember as if it were yesterday. The first day of Bajram was the 11th of June, and on the 10th of June, Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic, while on the road in the location called Gajic, he was going along the road, along that road in a green Zastava car. Somebody else was driving while Mitar was sitting in the passenger's seat, carrying a black flag with skull and bones on it, and he was calling out to Muslims to -- he was yelling out from the car, "Muslims, we are distributing Kurban meat tomorrow." That happened on the 10th of June, that is, the day before Kurban Bajram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does part of the Muslim celebration of Kurban Bajram involve a special meat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: According to the customs and the Muslim tradition, is that, for example, if you have a parent who died recently and who passed it on to his brother or sister to slaughter sheep then, that can be done for the immediate kin or on behalf of those who died, and then the meat is distributed amongst relatives, which is usually done in the afternoon hours on the first or the second day of Kurban Bajram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the 14th of June. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: The 14th of June was the fourth day of Kurban Bajram, which is celebrated for four days. The festivities last four days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before I move on, I just want to ask you one question to clear up something. The village of Gajic that you've referred to, can you describe where that is in relation to Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It is situated before Kosovo Polje, on the road to Visegrad, some 200 or 300 metres away from it. There is a little hill there from the direction of Kosovo Polje towards Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with where the village of Koritnik is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that in relation to where you were staying in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Koritnik is situated on the road to Sase Pod Greben and you have to turn right off the road to reach Koritnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, did there come a time when you saw a group of people on the road in front of Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Around noon. There was a large group of people consisting of some 50 or 60 people, including men, women, and children, and they were carrying - I don't know how to describe it - some bags and bundles, small bags and the like. And [redacted] was amongst them. She used to be our neighbour. She lived some 200 metres away from Kosovo Polje but still in the part which belongs to Kosovo Polje. She was with her relatives, because she is also from the Kurspahic family, but she had built her house near Kosovo Polje. So she joined them and she was going towards the town with them. She only came to get some clothes, and she told me that they were going to join a convoy for Olovo, so they were at that point in time heading towards Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any conversation with any members of this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I did not talk to them, but I did speak to Igbala, because up until the 14th, she was living in Kosovo Polje. She was spending a lot of time in Kosovo Polje, actually. She had two sisters there, where she was staying at the time, because she had fled from her house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on that day, did you have occasion to see Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you see him with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: So on the first day of Kurban Bajram, on the 11th, and then until the 14th of June, a lot of Muslims were slaughtered and destroyed in Visegrad. I could see that with my own eyes, because the Drina River is some hundred metres away from my house. There was blood in the river and bodies were floating on the surface of the Drina. Since I have two daughters -- there were a lot of women, maybe 10 or 12 young girls. We were trying to move those young women away, so we were withdrawing from the area of Gajic, some 50 metres away from there, and there were 10 or 12 of us there at one point in time. And I saw a Passat car passing by. Because at that time we knew that the car belonged to a woman by the name of Bahija [phoen], and according to the statements of witnesses, she was killed by Milan Lukic. And Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic came out of that car together with Milan Lukic and another individual unknown to me who was wearing a JNA uniform. And it was at that moment that we saw Igbala Kurspahic -- no. Sorry. I apologise. No. That was on the 9th of June. Sorry, I have to concentrate a little. Yes. We saw Mitar and Milan then, together with another individual, and Professor (redacted) came by. He's a short man, wears glasses. He couldn't see anything without his glasses. And they were arguing on the road. We were in one of the bushes near the road. And they pushed Rasim into the car and drove him in the direction of Visegrad. I don't know what happened to Rasim after that, but he hasn't been seen ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the colour of this car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately what time did this occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Around 6.00 p.m. Later in the day, at sunset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned Milan Lukic. Can you describe for us how it is you know this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I have known Milan Lukic ever since he was a child. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe how Mr. Lukic was dressed on this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: On that day, he was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I saw a weapon on Lukic on that occasion, but I didn't notice that Mr. Vasiljevic had any weapon on that particular occasion. But I did see the man being pushed into the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third man that you've described, did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: He had a rifle. I don't know what kind of rifle it was, but he was carrying it across his shoulder, slung on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these three men have any disguise or covering over their face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: He had a cap which was covering his face, with holes for eyes and his mouth. It was black in colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which person had this covering on his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's the person that you did not recognise who had his face covered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court where you were when you were making these observations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Let me think. I can't remember the names of these various paramilitary formations. At a certain point in time, we wanted to hide the girls and the young women in a building, in some bushes, because whenever they broke into villages, they didn't dare go into the meadows or the creeks or the streams so they would just go into a small path, and whoever they found, they would either kill them or take them away or ask them to lead them to others who were in hiding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where exactly were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: We were on the right-hand side, next to the property of a neighbour of mine, because there were some trees there, some small trees, and we were hiding there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate for the Court the distance between you and the red Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Just below the road, maybe 20 or 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look down on your sheet of paper there. I'm going to ask you: Did there come a time when you saw Witness number 13 after this event that you have just described for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've lost the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. I failed to switch on my microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want the witness to repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If possible, yes, or I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got it there? You sufficiently noted it to be able to repeat it without having to repeat the evidence itself?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: She was saying that between 4.00 and 4.30 a.m., between the 16th and the 17th of June, without getting to the verb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it that you saw Witness number 13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Let me repeat: This happened between the 16th and the 17th, about 4.00 a.m. or 4.30 a.m. I was sleeping, and my neighbours knocked on my door. They said, "Can you come and bandage a woman?" I know that there was no shooting in our neighbourhood that night, so I was surprised. How come there was a woman wounded who needed treatment? So I got up. I had some bandages. I went outside. I saw in front of me the person number 13. Person number 13 was wearing a lady's vest, but it was covered in dried blood, and she had tights. Her feet -- she didn't have any shoes on. She was holding her left arm and she was wounded in the thigh, I think it was of her left thigh. She asked us to give her first aid. At the time, she looked like a witch, to put it that way. Her hair was on end, untidy; she was dirty. I took her into the cornfield, I washed her and we cut her hair because you couldn't comb through it, put a comb through it. I just managed to put a bandage on her arm. However, it was warm at the time - the weather was warm - and there were a hundred flies that collected around this bandage, like a beehive, so you couldn't approach her four or five metres away. I took her back to the cornfield. I gave her another bath. I washed her again. However, when I removed the bandage, the muscles were falling out. The bone had been broken and there was pus everywhere. And I asked my neighbours for their help. We believed in a particular plant which needed to be put on the wound. Then I took some antibiotics out and put some powder there, but that didn't help either. I bandaged the arm again and I asked them to bring some pure alcohol, because my mother was a sick woman and she used alcohol for her feet. And they brought half a glass of alcohol and I poured it onto this wound. In a couple of minutes, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I saw worms that were more than a centimetre long, white worms. I put some plum twigs and pulled out, worm by worm, five or six of them. We found a piece of wood and we put it under her arm, and again I found this plant, I squeezed it and, with the juice, I covered the wound and bandaged it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how much time did you spend with this woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: The third day, we left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known this woman before you met her this night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: At first I couldn't recognise her, because she had changed so much. Her face had gone black, perhaps because of the bleeding. But when she told me whose daughter-in-law she was, I knew her in-laws very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did she know you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Later she remembered. When I told her who I was, then she remembered me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you who did this to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: At the time, she told me everything. As far as I'm able to recollect, she said that they had been chased out of Koritnik, allegedly to go for the convoy to Olovo. They were taken to Pionirska Street, to one house then to another. Then apparently Mr. Mitar came and Mr. Milan Lukic and Bosko Djuric, that they had forced them into a house, that they had shot -- that they had set the house alight, that she, with her son, this person number 13, had managed to jump out the window, but at the time she never knew whether her son had survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after your treatment of Witness number 13, did you ever see Mr. Vasiljevic again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When is the next time you saw Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: On the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us the circumstances under which you saw him at that time? I'm sorry, let me ask you this first: At what time on the 18th of June? Can you approximate for us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It was about 1800 hours, so late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you observe him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I asked a Serb neighbour of mine to drive me home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it would be helpful, I think, if we had some idea from the witness why she is certain that it was that date or that it was after the previous event or something like that. It is rather important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why it is you say that this day was the 18th of June? How is it that you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Because the things we lived through in Kosovo Polje were intolerable. Ten to twenty various groups would break into the village on a daily basis. Some were looking for jewellery, some for German marks, some for money. They killed, they slaughtered, they set houses on fire so we could no longer stand it. And on the 19th of June, in the evening, we officially decided, we got together in a stream and we officially decided to cross from the right bank of the Drina to the left bank of the Drina and to look for salvation in the woods. And I know exactly that it was on the 18th of June I asked my neighbour to take me home because I had been thrown out of my house without anything. So I wanted to get some clothes and food to feed my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you back to the 18th. Can you describe the circumstances surrounding your observation of Mr. Vasiljevic on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Mitar knows very well on the 18th of June that he came to Kosovo Polje with Milan Lukic. Milan killed Nurka Kos. Next to Murka -- Nurka, he tore up the ID card of a man, and the children brought it and we glued it together so we were able to see who the man was. So next to the killed Nurka Kos, he left this ID card in shreds. This happened -- 14, 16 -- at 17 or 1800 hours. But since there was a lot of shooting about 300 metres away from us, in the creek called Sase - this went on for days and nights - I went with person number 98, my intention being to prepare some beans, the planting of beans. It's not far. It's just around a bend. And there was Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and another man. And in front of them were four civilians whom I couldn't recognise. This was, after all, 150 to 200 metres away. They shot at them, they killed them, and they fell into the Drina River. I went back and told my neighbours about this and that night, we firmly decided that on the 19th of June we should leave Kosovo Polje and go to the left bank of the Drina. But in the morning, when we went to another neighbour to ask what we should do - the neighbour's name was [redacted], and he said, "Dig in. We can't help you any more. Lukic's gang was killed Stankoka Pecikoza." That was on the 19th of June. So we went back and we managed to collect a hundred or 120 people. We had a boat which had been shot at and there were holes from bullets. But the men found a way to stop up those holes and, at 2.00 in the morning, we crossed the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you back to your description of what you observed. You said that you were approximately 100 to 200 metres away and was not able to recognise the victims. How is it you were able to recognise the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you know someone for 20 years and even more than 20 years, and if you see a man up to ten times a day, like I did Mitar, and Mitar knows very well where I worked and that we went to eat there, that he served us, and we often sat together and had a drink and had fun together, then you can recognise him, no matter how many metres away he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 19th, when you crossed the Drina River, would you describe for the Court the condition of the river at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I wouldn't like any one of you to see such a scene. There was a boat that I said was riddled with holes, and it took a lot of effort to be able to use it. And I was the first to enter the boat, carrying my daughters. As we were crossing the Drina, we had to push away dead bodies with the oars so that the boat could move. Some were hanging on trees, some were on the shallow end, and I had to hold my nose. When I got out, my husband asked me where the children were, and I was not aware that they were not with me in the boat. And that night we all crossed to the Jelacic village, the neighbouring Bosniak village close to Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you crossed over the Drina on this day, did there ever come a time when you had to cross back over the Drina and return to Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes. Being a woman, I crossed three times - but my husband wouldn't let me cross again after that - because we hadn't taken anything with us. All we cared about was to save our lives and the lives of our children. I crossed back for the first time on the 21st of June, the second time on the 23rd of June, and for the last time on the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the 21st of June, and can you describe for us what, if anything, you saw from Kosovo Polje on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I apologise to Your Honours. May I address Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic in answering this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, madam, it would be best if you just answer the question. I don't want to be difficult, but it would be provocative and unnecessarily so. So just answer the question that counsel has asked you and we'll get along a lot more happily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe to the members of the Court what it was that you observed when you crossed --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I crossed, on the 21st of June, we went to get some food, because our village had still not been burnt down. A man called Selim Musanovic, he had brought large quantities of beehives to Kosovo Polje. At the time, we didn't have sugar and we went to collect the honey from those beehives. This was after 2200 hours. Mitar came along from the direction of Sase. He was tipsy, with a rifle on his shoulder, and he was with Veljko Planincic, also known as Razonoda, a former policeman. They were singing various songs about the Bosniaks and they went off, probably in the direction of Mitar's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far away were you from Mr. Vasiljevic at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Maybe about 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did he see you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: He couldn't have seen us, because they were armed, they were singing, they were tipsy, and these beehives are rather large, maybe as big as this table, and we hid behind them until they passed, singing. And right next to them was the Orthodox cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned two other occasions that you crossed the river. On either of these occasions did you see Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: The last time that I saw Mitar was the 25th of June. He was walking alone. He was tipsy, with a rifle. He was passing through Kosovo Polje. He was singing songs. He would first pass the Serbian cemetery, then the Bosniak cemetery. He was coming from the direction of Sase on the 25th of June. That was the last time I crossed the Drina River to go to Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far away were you from him at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It is very close. I always said 10 or 15 metres. It may be 20 or 30, because if you come across someone with a rifle or something, all you do is to hide. I wasn't alone. There would always be 20 or 30 of us crossing the river to bring food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 81, as you sit here today, is there any doubt in your mind that you saw Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic after you treated Witness VG13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Let me say once again: I'm telling the truth. Right up until the 25th of June, 1992, I personally, and others, saw Mitar Vasiljevic coming from the direction of Sase, going towards Visegrad and passing through Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 81. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. Cross-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, in answer to Mr. Groome's question and Judge Hunt, I think that the dates you mentioned, the 19th, the 21st, 23rd, and the 25th, and the other ones, the 18th, the 14th to the 18th, that you are quite certain of these dates, linking everything to your crossing of the Drina, which occurred on the 19th of June, in the evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to wait for the transcript. So relying on this date, the 19th, when you talk about the 21st, the 23rd, and so you are saying it is two days after you crossed, four days, and so on. Is that how -- am I correct in interpreting your memory of those dates as being two, four, and six days after you had crossed the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also explained, madam, that on the 19th of June you went to the [redacted] house and learnt that he was killed, but I didn't understand quite who told you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I and another three people who went to visit [redacted], with whom we never had any problems, and we still don't, and [redacted] said, [redacted] was killed this morning at 6.00 a.m. They were supposed to take some money. Lukic and his gang killed him. Dig yourself in into the ground, because we can no longer help you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: They were probably the close relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day was it when you learnt about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: We first went sometime about 8.00 the first time, and the second time he told us, "Come around 10.00 and I will tell you the real truth," and that is when he said, "Please dig into the ground because we can no longer help you." That is verbatim what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're, of course, talking about half past 7.00 in the morning and 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: If I was talking about 10.00 in the evening, I would have said 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was at 10.00 that he gave you the whole truth. What did he tell you at half past 7.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Will you let me finish for the transcript, please. We have to make breaks between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did he tell you the first time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, because you and counsel are speaking the same language, there's a problem in relation to the translations. We are receiving your evidence translated into English and into French, and the interpreters have to be able to keep up with you. So would you please pause before you answer the question, just as Mr. Domazet is pausing before he asks you a question. In that way, the interpreters can keep up and we don't lose anything that you say. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me go back to this question. You said you went there twice, first at -- was it 7.30 or 8.30? It doesn't matter. What were you told the first time and what were you told the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: [redacted], who is still alive, told us the first time, "It seems that Lukic and his gang have killed [redacted]. Come around 10.00 and I will be able to tell you the truth."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And at 10.00, he told you that he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes. [redacted] told us at 10.00, [redacted] has been killed. We can no longer help you. Dig into the ground," and we turned back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you still in Kosovo Polje [redacted] body was brought to his house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: On the 19th of June, [redacted], the deceased, was not brought there. We just watched from a distance of some 300 metres, from the Drina, friends and neighbours and citizens coming to express their condolences to the family of [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So you did not see a car bringing his body.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It was not on that day, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And the next day, you were no longer in Kosovo Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: In the evening, at 2200 hours, we crossed from the right bank of the Drina to the left bank of the Drina, and found accommodation in the Bosniak village of Jelacic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were watching the funeral, did they tell you when that was, when it was that he was buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: See, while we were in that village, hundreds of shells were falling down every day, so we did not have time to think of anything else but how to get some food and save the lives of ourselves and our children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I therefore interpret your answer as meaning that nobody told you that, that is, that you didn't know when [redacted] was buried, nor the day when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I know that some people watched the funeral, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it was on the 21st that you returned for the first time, in the evening hours of the 21st, that is, two days after you had learned about [redacted]. Does that help you in any way? Does it mean that it was after his funeral or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Once again, sir, I have to tell you that I don't know the date when late [redacted] was buried, but it was on the 21st that I first returned to the [redacted] to get some food for my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was on that day that you said you saw this large group of men taking honey from the beehive belonging to the individual that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes, including myself and a couple of other women and Bosniak men, because we didn't have any sugar. We wanted to use the honey to take it to the left bank of the Drina River so that we have something to eat, to survive on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you all together while crossing the river? Did you cross it by boat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: We crossed the river in two or three groups, in boats which were completely packed, because we had to be at the river, by the river, at a specific time so that we could cross over together at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the men who were with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Well, you're asking too much. I really cannot tell you the names now. I don't want to mention the names now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that you do remember the names but that for various reasons you don't wish to tell them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I am a hundred per cent sure about the names, but I do not wish to mention them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, I remind you, please do pause before you answer the question. You came straight in after the question there, understandably, but you must try and pause, otherwise we lose some of your evidence. I think the interpreters were able to catch up this time, but they can't always. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell the Court the reasons why you decline to tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I am not required to give you or the Court the reasons why I do not wish to disclose the identity of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let me go back to the events that you describe took place on the 19th of June, before the death of Stanko Pecikoza and before you crossed the river Drina. You said that the day before that, that is, on the 18th of June, you had seen Mitar Vasiljevic on two occasions. Once you saw him in the afternoon hours, in Sase, and the second time in Kosovo Polje, when Milan Lukic killed Nurka Kos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure about the way and the time it happened? Are you sure that it had taken place before you crossed the Drina River, that is, before you learnt about the death of Stanko Pecikoza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second occasion, you said you observed him from a somewhat greater distance, and you said that you had gone to a field to pick some plants. The location in question is quite a way from your village, the creek in Sase, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: If you listened carefully to the interpretation, you could realise that it was not very far from the area where I was born, because the man in question was, after all, someone I had known for many years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was not my question. You already explained that to the Court. You said you were able to recognise the individuals from a hundred or 200 metres' distance and you gave us the reasons for that. I just wanted to know how it came about that you happened to be near the brook, near the creek in Sase, because it was far away from Kosovo Polje where you were on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: If you are familiar with Kosovo Polje and Visegrad, from the Kalate community centre up until the village of Sase, the whole area belongs to Muslims, Bosniaks. They have their properties there near Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm quite familiar with the area in question. Of course I do not know the owners of the property there, but my question concerned the actual distance, because on that day you were hiding in the village, and it was on the same day that you went very far, because the creek in Sase, as you will agree with me, is far away from Kosovo Polje, especially when you go on foot and especially if you bear in mind the fact that you were in hiding on that day. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: You're not right at all, because throughout that period of time, from the month of April until the 19th of June, it was not possible for a Bosniak to move freely around the area. We were all looking for a hole to hide. And the Drina River is very near that area. And if you should try to walk along the river on that portion of the territory, you will see that it is quite possible to observe the surroundings with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely the reason for my question. I know that one can easily observe the area in question, but I would like to know whether it was possible for you on that day, after a very serious incident that you had witnessed, to go, to dare and go to the Sase creek, together with the individuals who were, like yourself, quite visible there. And you have explained us that you were in hiding in those days, that you were afraid.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I didn't tell you that I was at the creek in Sase but that I was some two or three hundred metres away from it. If you should become interested as to the whereabouts of my property, you can go to the land registry service to find out for yourself. But I simply had to go there. I had to go and forage for food to help my family survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, both of you, you must pause. You really must. Now, madam, I know this is probably the first time you have had to worry about this, but it is impossible for the interpreters to keep up when you answer the question straight away. Now, you came in straight away after the question, and it was a very long question and it was a very long answer. So I really must insist that you do keep in mind the need to pause. Mr. Domazet, you came in with a question pretty quickly there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you spoke about the incident which had taken place before this one, that is, the arrival of Witness VG13 in your house, you told us that it had taken place between the 16th and the 17th of June, in the early morning hours, around 4.00 a.m. Does that mean that it took place in the night of that day, that it took place on the 17th, at 4.00, that that was the first time you met with that witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It took place in the early morning hours, at about 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what we discussed about the date, does that mean that that took place two days after your crossing over of the Drina River on the 19th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Stop. Just stop. May I suggest to you, madam, that you watch the screen in front of you -- just check to see that the transcript is showing, will you? You'll see a transcript being typed in front of you on the screen. When you see the typing stop, that is the time to answer the question. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Domazet. You'll have to ask the question again, I think. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat the question, madam. My question concerned the basis on which you concluded these dates, linking them to the 19th of June, when you crossed the Drina. Can we conclude that your sighting of Witness VG13, which you said took place in the night between the 16th and the 17th of June, at 4.00 a.m., was two days before you crossed the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Once again, I have to say that it is very difficult for me to remember. Ten years have gone by. But I know that it took place two or three days, not more than that, because the person VG13 didn't stay longer than that in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to the incident that you described took place five days before the crossover, the incident involving Rasim Torohan. Could you explain to us in greater detail where you and others who were with you were at the time you witnessed this incident, as you described it today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I've already said that, and if you listened carefully, you were able to hear everything and record everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, may I suggest that if there is any particular matter about which you want further detail, you ask her about it. It was a very general question. I think you'll get perhaps a more helpful attitude if you ask her specifically in relation to any particular matter. This is the professor, is it, who couldn't see? Perhaps you could ask her step-by-step through the story she told.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, were you present in the field called Gajici, that is, in the area which is situated immediately next to the road leading from Visegrad to Prelovo? Were you in that particular field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified today that you were hiding there with some other individuals. Where exactly were you hiding? Behind what structure, under what structure? Could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I think I have already explained that and described how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the crop on that field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: [redacted] One part of it was grass, one part of the field was maize, then I also had some carrots there, I remember, onions, and on the right-hand side there were some bushes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, when you said that "on the right-hand side," do you mean looking from the road or from some other vantage point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Well, I think that as you look from the direction of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your field situated below or above the road Visegrad-Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Below the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that part of the village, is Rasim Torohan's house situated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes. It was nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his brother's house located there as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those houses located between the Visegrad-Prelovo road and the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Near the section of the road leading to Sase, Visegrad-Sase road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Visegrad-Sase. But between that road and the river, and the Drina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is his brother's house near the road, more towards the road, behind Hasim [as interpreted] Torohan's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: His brother's house is closer to the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us: When you saw Rasim Torohan, where exactly was he in relation to the houses? Was he on the road, level with the houses? Was he moving towards, in the direction of Visegrad? Where exactly was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Rasim was going towards Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the car, the red Passat car driven by Milan Lukic? Was it driving in the same direction or in the opposite direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: When they took him, they drove him in the direction of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but my question concerned the direction in which the car was moving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: The car was driving ahead of the car where I was, from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were able to observe that from your field, from the spot where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer my question with yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I have to apologise because I made a mistake. I linked it up with another incident which took place on the 9th of June. I was able to see everything that was going on, that is, when he was stopped, when they were arguing, when he dropped his glasses, and when he was pushed into the Passat car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the weather was like that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It's hard for me to remember when my father died. Sometimes I have to ask my sister about the date of his death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, madam, but it seems to me that your memory is very well in respect of certain other things that you've been testifying about, so I thought that you might be able to remember the details concerning that particular day as well. However, if you cannot remember, I will not insist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: If I should start telling you about the details, you know ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, would you please answer my questions. You lived for a very long time in that area, in that ethnically mixed area, so I'm sure you are familiar with some ethnic customs of Serbs. Is it customary for Serbs, for individuals who are in mourning, to sing songs as part of that custom? Is that a Serbian tradition or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I know that they are moaning, they're wailing while at the cemetery, during funerals. I don't know about singing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about the first time, that is, when you spoke about the departure of the Uzice Corps, you said that you were stopped in front of Mitar Vasiljevic's house by himself, his wife, and three other uniformed individuals. Do you remember, since you were in front of that house, what the gate of the house looked like, of Mitar Vasiljevic's house, that is? Could you describe it, if that was indeed the location where the incident happened, as you told us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, it was a simple wooden gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the vicinity of that house during the time when the Uzice Corps was there, there was a checkpoint or a barricade where soldiers controlled the traffic? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes, but it was further below Mitar's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in the vicinity of his house, is that correct, near the house? Madam, I asked you whether it was near the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: It was not very near Mitar's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One further question: Before Mitar Vasiljevic's arrest, did you ever give a statement to any official authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the MUP, or maybe to the investigators of the Prosecutor's office, or was it only after his arrest that you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I don't have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam. This concludes my cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you've accepted each time she said she didn't have to answer something. If you want a direction, you're entitled to seek it. It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, except for this, Mr. Domazet: If you want to later on ask the Prosecution to accept there's something in her statement which is to the contrary of her evidence, then you have an obligation to put it to the witness herself. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. And you don't want to get an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can I ask her after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. If you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- obtain an acceptance from the Prosecution that there is some inconsistent statement, you have an obligation to put that inconsistent statement to the witness to enable her, if she wishes to, to explain it or to say it's wrongly recorded or whatever. So I think that if you do want to follow that procedure, you will have to ask her the question and I will tell her she has to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then, Your Honour. My intention was to do it somewhat later in the proceedings. I will ask the Prosecutor to agree that in the statement that she gave to the investigator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think you've understood the problem that I am raising with you. As counsel, and as a matter of fairness, you have an obligation to put an inconsistent statement to the witness if you want to rely upon it later, to give the witness an opportunity of dealing with that inconsistent statement. We're all very well aware of the way in which these statements are taken and the problems that all the translations -- that the procedure goes through, but I think that the fair thing, for you to rely upon it, is to give her the opportunity of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness is refusing to answer those questions concerning individuals who may have been witnesses to what she described today, and I tried to elicit something more about it from the witness, in particular, concerning the incidents that took place between the 14th and the 19th of June, and even after that date, but the witness either avoided those answers or specifically indicated that she didn't want to answer those questions, I don't see any way to pursue the matter further and to insist thereupon, because it is obvious that such is her wish. However, if there is a way, some other way, some other possibility for those names to be mentioned, the names that she refused to indicate, I should like it to be done. I should like to ask for that permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, what she said at the time was, "I don't have to answer that question," when you asked her who they were. If you had asked me, I would have told the witness that she does have to answer them, and if she doesn't, a great deal less weight will be given to her evidence, because she is denying you the opportunity of testing that evidence, and I'm sure the witness would understand the reasonableness of that. If she has a particular problem with identifying these people, we want to know what that problem is. There may be ways around that problem, and if there aren't, at least we have an explanation. But the attitude which the witness has demonstrated to a number of questions you've asked demonstrates that she believes that she does not have to answer them. I would explain to her, if you asked me to, why she should answer them. But it would be unfair to her not to give her the opportunity of explaining these things so that when we come, in the end, to judge what weight should be given to her evidence, we have that explanation. If she refuses to give that explanation, unfortunately, she will be told that we will have to give less weight to her evidence than we otherwise would have. Now, it's a matter for her whether she wants to help us or not. If she doesn't want to help us, then her evidence will be given less weight. Now, It's after 11.00. I'll simply just explain that to the witness and we'll come back to it after the adjournment. Now, madam, you are here to help the Tribunal, I assume, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am here, but I simply cannot tell the names of persons who will perhaps one day appear before the Court as witnesses. I don't wish to tell you their names or surnames. I can give that information to whoever needs it, but I cannot be as public and open towards the Defence. I cannot tell the names of potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you have a valid reason for not giving us their names, then that is a matter we can take into account in judging what weight is to be given to your evidence, but your belief that you can't give them is not sufficient. Now, if you want us to rely upon your evidence, you either give us the names or you give us a proper explanation as to why you can't give the names. It's not a question of who asks you the questions; it's a question of whether you want to help the Tribunal with your evidence. Now, we'll give you some time to think about it. We're going to adjourn until 11.35, and when we resume, either we want you to give us your names or we get from you a valid explanation as to why you can't do it. Merely because the Defence asks, may I suggest to you, is not a valid reason. We'll adjourn now until 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, madam, there are two problems that we have here. First of all, we can understand your diffidence or your wish not to disclose the identity of certain persons, but we do have to know the reasons for it. And I can see no reason why you can't give us those reasons. That's the first thing. The second thing is, you were asked, Did you make a statement to the Prosecution's investigator, and you said you didn't have to answer that question either. Well, that is something you do have to answer. We know very well you made a statement to the Prosecution's investigator. We haven't seen it, but we know you've made one. Then you will be asked, in relation to that, didn't you say something in that statement? Now, my guess is it's something which is inconsistent with what you've already said in evidence here, and there may be a very good reason why you have said something different to what is recorded in that statement. And it is very important, from our point of view, to know why it was different, if it was in fact different, because it may be a very reasonable explanation, and we need to know that in order to know what weight to give to your evidence. Now, it's very important. We have to judge what weight to be given to your evidence because it's going to be contradicted by people being called by the Defence, and we have to, in the end, decide whether your evidence should be accepted. Now, we want to help you to help us, and if your evidence is going to be accepted, we can only be helped by you if you tell us these things. Now, first of all, in relation to the men that were with you on the boat crossing the Drina, that was the first one, wasn't it, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, you say you don't want to reveal their identity. Can you explain to us why you don't want to? What is it you fear? For their safety or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I didn't understand that the question was about the men who were crossing the boat. I understood it to be the men on the 18th who were looking when Rasim was taken away. As for the men who were crossing in the boat on the 19th, there's no problem there. On that day, the whole population of Kosovo Polje crossed the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that when you were speaking of some men on the boat, it just was part of the population of your locality or place where you used to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one boat that would cross, and then it would come back to pick up another group, and it maybe made three or four crossings, because 150 people couldn't get into one boat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, then, if you were asked to name some of those persons, you would be able to do so; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can remember some names, judging by the households, the names of the people who crossed on the 19th of June. So if necessary, I can name the households, the families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the second thing was in relation to the statement which you gave. Now, you said you didn't want to answer that. Do you understand now that you really should answer that question and you will then be asked some questions about what is recorded in that statement? Are you prepared to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean on the 19th, the people crossing by boat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I myself do not know what it is that Mr. Domazet wants to ask you about, but he will want to put to you something which is recorded in this statement as having been said by you to the Prosecution's investigators. Now, do you have any problem with answering those questions? You'll be shown the document, if you need to have it, to check what is written in it, but you had said previously you weren't going to answer those questions. Are you able to say now that you will answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I would ask you for your assistance again, because a moment ago, when you put your first question to the witness, the witness answered that she could give the names of the people who crossed by boat on the 19th to the other bank of the Drina River. But that was not my question. I was not referring to those men on the 19th of May. I was referring to those who, two days later, were with her when they were collecting honey, and allegedly saw Mitar Vasiljevic and Planincic singing and walking along the road. The witness said that a group of men was with her, and my question was in relation to those men who were with her that evening, who they were, and not what the witness said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'm very sorry, but I did ask you whether that was what you were after and you gave me your assent. That's why I took it up with the witness. Now, you want, then, to these ones on the 19th of June -- was it the 19th of June? 21st of June. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the incident the 21 of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be glad to give the names of the men who were with me, but in view of the fact that I assume that those men will appear before the Tribunal, because of their personal safety and revealing their identity, I would not like to mention their names. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are these people witnesses in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm just going to ask if that the witness is going to name these people, that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, certainly, yes, but I'm still looking for it in the transcript as to when the question was asked. Have you got any reference to it, Mr. Domazet? I remember the questions, but I want to make sure that we're all talking about the same thing this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we've found it. It's at the end of page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's her evidence-in-chief, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. That's my mistake. We're looking for the cross now. Your Honours, it's at the top of page 41. Please disregard that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I think the first answer of the witness was on line 12 of page 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just on that page when I was diverted to 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Sorry. At the end of 25, not 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these are the questions:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was on that day that you said that you saw this large group of men taking honey from the beehive belonging to the individual that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes, including myself and a couple of other women and Bosniak men, because we didn't have any sugar. We wanted to use the honey to take it to the left bank of the Drina River so that we have something to eat, to survive on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you all together while crossing the river? Did you cross it by boat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: We crossed the river in two or three groups in boats which were completely packed because we had to be at the river, by the river, at a specific time so that we could cross over together at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the men who were with you on that occasion? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, is that the one that you're worried about, Mr. Domazet? That is the one that she declined to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly tied, as far as I can see it, to any particular incident of having seen your client. I'm glad to see that my recollection of it wasn't all that faulty, although I may have had the wrong crossing. If you want to pursue this issue, may I suggest you ask the questions again, the ones that you want answered, and then if the witness says she can't or does not wish to identify any particular person, we will then give her the opportunity of explaining why. But perhaps before you do that, I should say this to the witness: Is your fear that, by disclosing their names, they might be brought here as witnesses? Is that what you're worried about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not worried in the least as to the willingness of these people to say what they know here in the Tribunal, but if I were to give the names of those men who know what I know, I fear for their safety, because those men just now are down there and they are building their houses in Visegrad, or they are coming and going to visit what remains of their homes which were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I better put it to you directly: Are you concerned that there is somebody in Visegrad who may retaliate if they are going to give evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fear for every returnee, not just witnesses, because the situation in Visegrad is still far from civilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And they are returning to live in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are returning and they are building houses, and they are coming and going. And I do believe that every witness who is called and who has seen and knows what he knows will respond to a call from the Tribunal, and it is for those reasons that I would not like to give the first and last names of those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding you as saying that you believe that they would want to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who those witnesses are, but all those people who saw and experienced everything I know, and maybe more than that, will certainly come to the Tribunal to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you think that they are willing to give that evidence, what is your fear in revealing who they would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be quite frank, because that is my nature. If the Defence of Mr. Vasiljevic is here who can use his mobile telephone tonight and say the names of these people, then I fear that those witnesses, if they are witnesses, will not dare to come here, and they will have to abandon Visegrad for good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now I understand you. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Domazet. I realise there was an insinuation against you which is understandable, perhaps, to somebody who is ignorant of the responsibilities of counsel, but it's not only you who that fear would be related to. That is one of the problems that we face very regularly in this Tribunal. It means, of course, that the incident is untested, and for that reason it may, unless it's otherwise supported, may have less weight in the overall evidence in the case. But may I suggest that, first of all, you take her to her statement. I don't know whether there's anything in her statement about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but Mr. Groome is standing up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I offer just a practical solution. One possibility would be for, after the witness's testimony, to provide those names confidentially, and after the Prosecution has rested its case and in the break before the Defence case, the Prosecution would take steps to have these witnesses brought to the UN office in Sarajevo and make them available for Mr. Domazet to interview these people, if he would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that will meet the witness's concerns, but if you have any such suggestion, we can deal with that later. At the moment, from my own point of view, I would not ask the witness to identify them here in court, whatever may happen in other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, what about the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will ask the witness a few things in connection with her statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I have to ask once again, and I hope I will get an answer: Did you give a statement to the investigator of The Hague Tribunal in January this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give any statements or reports in connection with things that happened in Visegrad to anybody, any other institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: No one even dreamt that there would be this Tribunal, or any other, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was whether you gave a statement to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecution; once or several times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the statement in January of this year, when was the other one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I think both were in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is one and the same statement. And who did you make statements to prior to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG81
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to answer that question if I don't have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Madam, this is a very fair question to ask of you.
